subtitle: A 128-bit identifier that any machine can mint on its own, with no central office to ask.
summary: RFC 9562 defines the Universally Unique Identifier (UUID), a 128-bit value meant to be unique across space and time without any central registration. It covers versions 1 to 8 (version 2 is left to DCE) with different recipes: clock-based, name-hashed, random, and the new time-ordered versions 6 and 7. It also defines the Nil and Max UUIDs, the urn:uuid: namespace, and best practices for generating and storing them. It replaces RFC 4122.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9562 defines the Universally Unique Identifier (UUID), a 128-bit value meant to be unique without any central registration. It covers versions 1 to 8 (version 2 is left to DCE), including the new time-ordered versions 6 and 7. It also defines the Nil and Max UUIDs, the urn:uuid: namespace and best practices for generating and storing UUIDs. It replaces RFC 4122.

tldr.problem: Distributed systems need identifiers they can create independently, with no central authority and no risk of two machines picking the same one.
tldr.mechanism: A UUID is 128 bits with a variant field and a 4-bit version field; the other 122 bits come from a clock, a hash of a name, random data, or an application-defined layout depending on the version.
tldr.outcome: UUIDs are widely used to name database rows, files and events, and the new time-ordered UUIDv7 sorts by creation time, which keeps database indexes fast.

today: UUIDs are everywhere: database primary keys, object and file names, request and trace IDs, and the GUIDs of Microsoft Windows. UUIDv4 (random) is by far the most familiar, and the new UUIDv7 is being adopted as a sortable replacement for it as a database key. Many languages and databases have added UUIDv7 support since this RFC appeared in May 2024. The IANA registry at iana.org/assignments/uuid tracks UUID subtypes and namespace IDs.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A UUID, also called a GUID, is a 128-bit identifier. The RFC says it "requires no central registration process", so any machine can mint one at any time and expect it to be different from every other. The format has a long history: UUIDs started in the Apollo Network Computing System, were adopted by the Open Software Foundation's DCE, and then by Microsoft Windows.

RFC 9562 is the modern rewrite of the specification. It obsoletes RFC 4122, keeps versions 1 to 5 intact, and adds versions 6, 7 and 8. It also defines a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace so that a UUID can be written as urn:uuid:f81d4fae-7dec-11d0-a765-00a0c91e6bf6, building on RFC 8141.

An ITU-T Recommendation and an ISO/IEC standard (X.667) are derived from RFC 4122, and the RFC states that nothing in it overrides the DCE standards that first defined UUIDs.
sections.plainLanguage: A UUID, also called a GUID, is a 128-bit identifier that needs no central registration, so any machine can create one and expect it to differ from all others. RFC 9562 obsoletes RFC 4122, keeps versions 1 to 5 and adds versions 6, 7 and 8. It also defines a URN form, such as urn:uuid:f81d4fae-7dec-11d0-a765-00a0c91e6bf6.

sections.title: Motivation
sections.content:
The main appeal is that "no centralized authority is required to administer them". Generation can be fully automated, and the RFC says the algorithms support allocation rates of 10 million per second per machine or more. A fixed size of 128 bits is small enough to sort, hash and store easily.

The update exists because the world changed. Databases increasingly run on many machines, where auto-increment counters are hard to coordinate. But the older versions fall short for that use:

  • Random UUIDv4 values land at random places in a B-tree index, which hurts insert performance.
  • UUIDv1 uses an unusual 100-nanosecond epoch starting in 1582, and its fields are stored out of time order.
  • UUIDv1 embeds a MAC address, which leaks information about the machine.

The authors surveyed 16 existing time-sortable ID schemes (ULID, Snowflake, KSUID and others) before designing the new versions, and they folded in several RFC 4122 errata.
sections.plainLanguage: UUIDs need no central authority, can be generated automatically at rates of 10 million per second per machine or more, and fit in a fixed 128 bits. The update addresses problems with older versions. Random version 4 values scatter through database indexes and hurt insert speed. Version 1 stores its fields out of time order and embeds a MAC address, which leaks information about the machine.

sections.title: UUID Format: Variant and Version
sections.content:
Every UUID is 16 octets (128 bits), written most significant byte first. The usual text form is the "hex-and-dash" string of 32 hex digits in groups of 8-4-4-4-12, such as f81d4fae-7dec-11d0-a765-00a0c91e6bf6. Letters may be upper or lower case. The RFC recommends storing UUIDs in databases as 128-bit binary rather than text.

Two small fields decide how to read the rest. The variant sits in the most significant bits of octet 8 and selects the overall layout. All UUIDs in this RFC use the bit pattern 10, which shows up as a hex digit of 8, 9, A or B at the start of the fourth group. The version is the top 4 bits of octet 6 (bits 48 to 51), so it is the first digit of the third group.

Variant 10xx
The layout defined by this RFC. Other variants are reserved for Apollo NCS (0xxx), Microsoft (110x) and the future (111x).
Version nibble
Tells you the recipe: 1 Gregorian time, 3 MD5 name, 4 random, 5 SHA-1 name, 6 reordered time, 7 Unix time, 8 custom.
sections.plainLanguage: A UUID is 16 bytes, usually written as 32 hex digits in groups of 8-4-4-4-12, such as f81d4fae-7dec-11d0-a765-00a0c91e6bf6. Two small fields say how to read the rest. The variant, in the top bits of byte 8, selects the layout; this RFC uses bit pattern 10. The version, the first digit of the third group, names the recipe. Databases should store UUIDs as 128-bit binary.

sections.title: The UUID Versions
sections.content:
Section 5 gives each version its own bit layout, because the four rows of 32 bits are used differently by each recipe.

Version 1 holds a 60-bit timestamp counted in 100-nanosecond steps since 15 October 1582, a 14-bit clock sequence to survive clocks being set backwards, and a 48-bit node, usually an IEEE 802 MAC address. Version 6 has the same fields but stores the timestamp from most to least significant, so UUIDs sort by time. Version 7 is the one the RFC prefers: a 48-bit Unix millisecond timestamp followed by random data, with an optional counter or sub-millisecond fraction.

Versions 3 and 5 hash a namespace ID plus a name with MD5 or SHA-1, so the same name always gives the same UUID. Version 4 is 122 random bits. Version 8 leaves 122 bits to the implementation for custom or vendor use, and its uniqueness "MUST NOT be assumed". Version 2 (DCE Security) is out of scope.

The RFC says systems that do not involve legacy UUIDv1 SHOULD use UUIDv7 instead of UUIDv6, and that implementations SHOULD use UUIDv7 rather than UUIDv1 or UUIDv6 if possible. Where possible, UUIDv5 SHOULD be used in place of UUIDv3.
sections.plainLanguage: Each version builds the 128 bits differently. Version 1 uses a timestamp, a clock sequence and a node, usually a MAC address. Version 6 reorders the version 1 fields so UUIDs sort by time. Version 7 uses a Unix millisecond timestamp plus random data, and the RFC prefers it for new systems. Versions 3 and 5 hash a name, version 4 is random, and version 8 is for custom use.

sections.title: Nil and Max UUIDs
sections.content:
Two special values are defined. The Nil UUID has all 128 bits set to zero (00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000) and expresses "no such value here". The Max UUID has all 128 bits set to one (FFFFFFFF-FFFF-FFFF-FFFF-FFFFFFFFFFFF) and can act as a sentinel such as "end of UUID list".

Neither one uses the variant of this RFC: the Nil UUID falls in the Apollo NCS range and the Max UUID in the reserved future range. Name-based UUIDs have their own special inputs: four namespace IDs are listed (DNS, URL, OID and X500), for example the DNS namespace 6ba7b810-9dad-11d1-80b4-00c04fd430c8. Hashing the DNS namespace with the name www.example.com using MD5 gives the version 3 UUID 5df41881-3aed-3515-88a7-2f4a814cf09e once the version and variant bits are overwritten (see the RFC's Appendix A.2 for the exact arithmetic).
sections.plainLanguage: Two special values exist. The Nil UUID has all 128 bits set to zero and means "no such value here". The Max UUID has all bits set to one and can mark something like the end of a list. Name-based UUIDs start from one of four namespace IDs: DNS, URL, OID and X500.

sections.title: Best Practices
sections.content:
Section 6 is a toolbox of advice rather than strict rules, since "everything else is an implementation detail". Key points:

  • Monotonicity. To keep UUIDs generated in the same millisecond in order, implementations may use a fixed-length counter, a randomly seeded counter, or extra clock precision. Counters should be at least 12 and at most 42 bits.
  • Clock trouble. If the clock goes backwards or a counter rolls over, the generator should stall or report an error rather than knowingly return duplicates.
  • Randomness. Use a cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator (CSPRNG) where available.
  • No MAC address. To avoid identifying the host, use a random 48-bit node with the multicast bit set to 1, which no real network card address has.
  • Opacity. Treat UUIDs as opaque; parse them only when you must.
  • Databases. Store as 128-bit binary where possible, and avoid name-based UUIDs as primary keys.

The RFC also notes that sorting time-based UUIDs as raw bytes keeps related rows near each other in an index, which can be an order of magnitude better than random inserts.
sections.plainLanguage: Section 6 gives advice rather than strict rules. To keep UUIDs created in the same millisecond in order, implementations may use a counter or extra clock precision. If the clock goes backwards or a counter overflows, the generator should stall or report an error rather than return duplicates. Use a cryptographically secure random number generator, avoid real MAC addresses, and treat UUIDs as opaque.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
IANA now maintains two registries at iana.org/assignments/uuid: "UUID Subtypes" (the versions) and "UUID Namespace IDs". Old references to RFC 4122 in IANA registries, including the uuid URN namespace, were redirected to this document. New namespace IDs need Specification Required; the subtype table needs Standards Action.

UUIDs must not be treated as secrets. The RFC says implementations "MUST NOT" use them as security capabilities, meaning identifiers whose mere possession grants access.

Other cautions: a predictable random source makes UUIDs guessable; a human cannot spot a slightly altered UUID by eye; MAC addresses in UUIDs are a privacy risk and SHOULD NOT be used; and embedded timestamps reveal creation order. If UUIDs are used for any security purpose, UUIDv4 SHOULD be used. MD5 and SHA-1 have known weaknesses, covered in RFC 6151 and RFC 6194.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps two registries at iana.org/assignments/uuid: UUID Subtypes (the versions) and UUID Namespace IDs. UUIDs must not be treated as secrets or used as security capabilities, meaning identifiers whose possession grants access. A predictable random source makes UUIDs guessable, MAC addresses are a privacy risk, and embedded timestamps reveal creation order. For security purposes use version 4.

fields.name: unix_ts_ms
fields.desc: 48-bit big-endian Unix Epoch timestamp in milliseconds. Occupies bits 0 through 47.

fields.name: ver
fields.desc: The version field, set to 0b0111 (7). Occupies bits 48 through 51.

fields.name: rand_a
fields.desc: 12 bits of pseudorandom data, or an optional sub-millisecond fraction or counter for monotonicity.

fields.name: rand_b
fields.desc: The final 62 bits of pseudorandom data, or an optional counter.
